issues.title: Support `bytearray` in Dynamo
issues.author: guilhermeleobas
issues.body:
`bytearray` has no `VariableTracker` model in Dynamo and any attempt to use it will result in a graph break. We want to close this gap as `bytearray` seems to be used by some libraries under the hood. 

## Current state

Probed on `main` with `torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)`.
Each row is roughly `torch.compile(lambda b: <op>, backend="eager",
fullgraph=True)(bytearray(b"abc"))`.

| operation | result |
| --- | --- |
| `bytearray()` / `bytearray(3)` / `bytearray([1,2,3])` / `bytearray(b"abc")` / `bytearray("abc", "utf-8")` | `Unsupported: Failed to trace builtin operator` |
| pass a `bytearray` arg straight through | works |
| `b == b"abc"` | works |
| `isinstance(b, bytearray)` | works |
| `len(b)` | `Unsupported: C-implemented special method without VariableTracker model` |
| `b[1]`, `b[1:]`, `b[0] = 65` | same as above |
| `iter(b)` / `list(b)`, `98 in b` | same as above |
| `b.append(65)`, `b.extend(b"cd")`, `b += b"cd"` | `Unsupported: Failed to trace builtin operator` |
| `bytes(b)`, `memoryview(b)` | `Unsupported: Failed to trace builtin operator` |
| `b.decode()`, `b.hex()` | `Unsupported: Unsupported method call` |
| `b * 2` | `Unsupported: sq_repeat_impl not implemented` |
| mutating a `bytearray` passed in as an arg | `Unsupported: Unsupported method call` |
| `torch.frombuffer(b, dtype=torch.uint8)` | `Unsupported: Failed to convert args/kwargs to proxy` |
| `bytearray` subclass instantiation | `Unsupported: Unsupported function call` |

Three of the 26 probed operations work today.

## Scope of work
1. Port the CPython test suite
CPython has no `test_bytearray.py`; `bytearray` coverage lives in
`Lib/test/test_bytes.py` (~2657 lines), shared with `bytes` via a common base
class.

2. Add a `ByteArrayVariable(VariableTracker)` with support for sequence / mapping / number protocols, methods (using `tp_methods`), iteration, etc. Not everything needs to be done in the same PR and follow-ups are ok.

3. Fix the corner cases the port surfaces

issues.title: [inductor] solve_for_tiling raises AssertionError on nested ModularIndexing/FloorDiv expressions
issues.author: haojiang01
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch._inductor.tiling_utils.solve_for_tiling` crashes with an opaque `InductorError: AssertionError("expected no ModularIndexing or FloorDiv in expr")` when the index expression contains *nested* ModularIndexing, e.g.

    ModularIndexing(ModularIndexing(n0 - 252252, 1, 50), 1, 50)

This was observed in the fused backward kernel of a production recommendation model with cat/view-heavy indexing (#161819 does not cover this case). The error kills the whole compile.

Minimal deterministic repro (no GPU needed):

```python
import sympy
from torch._inductor import tiling_utils
from torch.utils._sympy.functions import ModularIndexing

n0 = sympy.Symbol("n0", integer=True, nonnegative=True)
inner = ModularIndexing(n0 - 252252, 1, 50)

print(tiling_utils.solve_for_tiling(inner))  # OK: 252253
print(tiling_utils.solve_for_tiling(ModularIndexing(inner, 1, 50)))  # AssertionError
```

### Root cause

`sympy.Basic.replace(Func, callback)` only peels ONE layer of a self-referential nested function per pass. With the div approximation `lambda x, y, z=None: x / y`, the outer match returns the original inner node unchanged (`inner / 1 == inner`), so a single pass yields `ModularIndexing(n0 - 252252, 1, 50)` and the subsequent check in `_solve_simple_expr`

    raise AssertionError("expected no ModularIndexing or FloorDiv in expr")

fires, killing the whole compile.

Pure-sympy demonstration of the one-layer-per-pass semantics:

```python
G = sympy.Function("G")
x = sympy.Symbol("x")
G(G(x, 1, 50), 1, 50).replace(G, lambda x, y, z=None: x / y)  # == G(x, 1, 50), residual left behind
```

### Proposed fix

1. Iterate the ModularIndexing/FloorDiv -> division approximation to a fixpoint (each pass strictly reduces the count of MI/FD nodes or makes no progress, so the loop terminates).
2. Replace the raise with a graceful `return None` ("cannot solve"), so any remaining unexpected residual degrades to "no tiling suggestion" instead of a hard compile failure. The final `sympy_subs(eq_1_expr, ...) == 1` check already validates any produced solution against the original expression.

PR incoming.

### Versions

Reproduced on current main (upstream main still carries the raise in `torch/_inductor/tiling_utils.py`, `_solve_simple_expr`). Originally hit on PyTorch 2.9 + #161819 backport in a 16-rank production training job; the fix has been validated there (compile succeeds, training runs normally).

comments.author: RohitRathore1
comments.body: it's an ordering bug, not flaky. `test_custom_op_symm_mem_realization` passes on its own but fails when the file or the whole LoweringTest class runs because Inductor generates the persistent symm-mem `alloc_id` with `random.randint(0, 2**64-1)` at codegen time and our test harness reseeds `random.seed(1234)` in `TestCase.setUp` before every test (common_utils.py), so the first randint draw is always the same value i.e., `14354624986284130233`, which isexactly the `alloc_id` in the traceback.. It's worth noting this isn't purely a test artifact since `alloc_id` comes from the globally-seeded random, any user code that calls `random.seed()` before `torch.compile()` on symm-mem collectives can hit the same collision. We should source `alloc_id` from `secrets.randbits(64)` instead of the global random as it only needs to be process-unique and is baked into the generated code as a constant, so entropy-based generation is both sufficient and immune to reseeding. Full `test_symmetric_memory.py` passes with it. PR coming shortly.

issues.title: [Inductor] AssertionError: len(index) == len(stride) in ir.py when using torch.compile(mode="max-autotune") on CPU BMM/GEMM
issues.author: xyt66665000
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When compiling an attention-like function containing complex numbers (`torch.polar`, `torch.view_as_complex`) and batched matrix multiplication (`torch.matmul`) on CPU with `torch.compile(mode="max-autotune")`, the compiler crashes with an `AssertionError`. 

The crash occurs during the C++ backend's BMM/GEMM template generation (`cpp_bmm_template.py`), specifically in the `indexer` function inside `torch/_inductor/ir.py` where it asserts `len(index) == len(stride)`.

A similar CUDA variant of this reproducer fails differently with KeyError: 'complex64' in Triton codegen.
I filed that separately because the failing backend path is different.

### Reproduction Script
```python
import torch

def target_function(
    l_tok_embeddings_weight_, l_tokens_, l_attn_norm_0_weight_, 
    l_wq_0_weight_, l_wk_0_weight_, l_wv_0_weight_, l_wo_0_weight_
):
    arange = torch.arange(0, 8, 2, device='cpu', dtype=torch.float32)
    angles = torch.true_divide(arange, 8)
    pow_1 = torch.pow(10000.0, angles)
    freqs = torch.true_divide(1.0, pow_1)
    t = torch.arange(0, 4, device='cpu', dtype=torch.float32)
    outer = torch.outer(t, freqs)
    freqs_1 = outer.float()
    ones_like = torch.ones_like(freqs_1)
    freqs_cis = torch.polar(ones_like, freqs_1)
    
    h = torch.nn.functional.embedding(l_tokens_, l_tok_embeddings_weight_)
    x_normed = h.float()
    pow_2 = x_normed.pow(2)
    mean = pow_2.mean(-1, keepdim=True)
    add = torch.add(mean, 1e-05)
    rsqrt = torch.rsqrt(add)
    x_normed_1 = torch.mul(x_normed, rsqrt)
    type_as = x_normed_1.type_as(h)
    normed_x = torch.mul(type_as, l_attn_norm_0_weight_)
    
    q = torch.nn.functional.linear(normed_x, l_wq_0_weight_)
    k = torch.nn.functional.linear(normed_x, l_wk_0_weight_)
    v = torch.nn.functional.linear(normed_x, l_wv_0_weight_)
    
    view = q.view(2, 4, 8, 8)
    q_1 = view.transpose(1, 2)
    view_1 = k.view(2, 4, 8, 8)
    k_1 = view_1.transpose(1, 2)
    view_2 = v.view(2, 4, 8, 8)
    v_1 = view_2.transpose(1, 2)
    
    float_3 = q_1.float()
    reshape = float_3.reshape(2, 8, 4, -1, 2)
    xq_ = torch.view_as_complex(reshape)
    
    float_4 = k_1.float()
    reshape_1 = float_4.reshape(2, 8, 4, -1, 2)
    xk_ = torch.view_as_complex(reshape_1)
    
    freqs_cis_1 = freqs_cis.reshape(1, 1, 4, -1)
    mul_2 = torch.mul(xq_, freqs_cis_1)
    view_as_real = torch.view_as_real(mul_2)
    xq_out = view_as_real.flatten(3)
    
    mul_3 = torch.mul(xk_, freqs_cis_1)
    view_as_real_1 = torch.view_as_real(mul_3)
    xk_out = view_as_real_1.flatten(3)
    
    q_2 = xq_out.type_as(q_1)
    k_2 = xk_out.type_as(k_1)
    
    mask = torch.full([1, 1, 4, 4], float('-inf'), device='cpu', dtype=torch.float32)
    mask_1 = torch.triu(mask, diagonal=1)
    transpose_3 = k_2.transpose(-2, -1)
    matmul = torch.matmul(q_2, transpose_3)
    
    scores = torch.mul(matmul, 0.35355339059327373)
    scores_1 = torch.add(scores, mask_1)
    attn_weights = torch.nn.functional.softmax(scores_1, dim=-1)
    attn_output = torch.matmul(attn_weights, v_1)
    
    transpose_4 = attn_output.transpose(1, 2)
    contiguous = transpose_4.contiguous()
    attn_output_1 = contiguous.view(2, 4, 64)
    linear_3 = torch.nn.functional.linear(attn_output_1, l_wo_0_weight_)
    
    return (arange, t, mask, h, angles, mask_1, x_normed, pow_1, pow_2, freqs, mean, outer, add, freqs_1, rsqrt, ones_like, x_normed_1, freqs_cis, type_as, freqs_cis_1, normed_x, q, k, v, view, view_1, view_2, q_1, k_1, v_1, float_3, float_4, reshape, reshape_1, xq_, xk_, mul_2, mul_3, view_as_real, view_as_real_1, xq_out, xk_out, q_2, k_2, transpose_3, matmul, scores, scores_1, attn_weights, attn_output, transpose_4, contiguous, attn_output_1, linear_3)


def get_inputs():
    torch.manual_seed(2077)
    return (
        torch.randn([512, 64], dtype=torch.float32) * 0.1,
        torch.zeros([2, 4], dtype=torch.int64),
        torch.randn([64], dtype=torch.float32) * 0.1,
        torch.randn([64, 64], dtype=torch.float32) * 0.1,
        torch.randn([64, 64], dtype=torch.float32) * 0.1,
        torch.randn([64, 64], dtype=torch.float32) * 0.1,
        torch.randn([64, 64], dtype=torch.float32) * 0.1,
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    inputs = get_inputs()
    
    print("Running torch.compile(mode='max-autotune')...")
    opt_fn = torch.compile(target_function, mode="max-autotune")
    
    try:
        opt_fn(*inputs)
        print("Compilation Passed (Bug not triggered).")
    except Exception as e:
        import traceback
        traceback.print_exc()
        print(f"\n[BINGO!] Crashed with: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
```

**Claude finished @jansel's task in 27s** —— [View job](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/29137749290)

---
### Answer

Yes. Autotuning benchmarks each candidate and picks the fastest, so on machines where the ATen `bmm` happens to win, the buggy CPP GEMM/BMM path is never codegen'd. To force the non-ATen (CPP) backend, restrict the GEMM backend list so ATen is not a candidate at all:

**Config:**
```python
import torch._inductor.config as config
config.max_autotune = True
config.max_autotune_gemm_backends = "CPP"   # drop ATEN/TRITON so only the CPP template is a choice
```

**Env var equivalent:**
```bash
TORCHINDUCTOR_MAX_AUTOTUNE=1 \
TORCHINDUCTOR_MAX_AUTOTUNE_GEMM_BACKENDS=CPP \
python bug.py
```

The default is `"ATEN,TRITON,CPP"` (see `torch/_inductor/config.py:648-650`). With only `CPP` in the list, autotuning has just the `cpp_CppMicroGemm*` choice, so it is selected regardless of measured timing — which should reproduce the `AssertionError: len(index) == len(stride)` in `ir.py`'s `indexer` deterministically, independent of the CPU/ISA.

Notes:
- On CPU you can drop `TRITON` (no effect), but keeping it in the list is harmless.
- If you additionally want to skip the benchmarking step entirely, `config.autotune_fallback_to_aten = False` combined with the above keeps ATen out of any fallback path too, though it isn't required just to force the CPP choice here.

issues.title: torch.compile silently produces wrong `nn.LayerNorm` results on MPS
issues.author: jstray
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.compile` returns numerically incorrect output for `nn.LayerNorm` on the MPS backend. Eager matches a float64 CPU reference to ~2e-7; the compiled version diverges by up to **1.8 absolute** on inputs whose own range is roughly [-4, 4] — the error exceeds the output range.

There is no warning, no graph break, and no device fallback. The compiled module simply returns wrong numbers.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
dim = 512
x = torch.randn(4, dim)
layer = nn.LayerNorm(dim)

reference = nn.LayerNorm(dim).double()
reference.load_state_dict({k: v.double() for k, v in layer.state_dict().items()})
truth = reference(x.double())                       # float64 CPU ground truth

on_mps = layer.to("mps").eval()
with torch.inference_mode():
    eager = on_mps(x.to("mps")).cpu().double()
    compiled = torch.compile(on_mps)(x.to("mps")).cpu().double()

print("eager    vs truth:", (eager - truth).abs().max().item())    # 3.3e-07
print("compiled vs truth:", (compiled - truth).abs().max().item()) # 1.8e+00
```

A self-contained script covering all dimensions and seeds is attached
(`bug_repro_mps_layernorm.py`).

## Expected behaviour

Both should agree with the float64 reference to float32 precision, ~1e-7.

## Actual behaviour

`max |output - float64_reference|`, three seeds per row:

| normalized_shape | eager | torch.compile |
|---|---|---|
| 32 | 1.2e-07, 2.4e-07, 2.4e-07 | 1.2e-07, 2.4e-07, 2.4e-07 |
| 64 | ~2e-07 | **1.7e-02**, 2.4e-07, **2.0e-02** |
| 96 | ~2e-07 | **6.7e-03, 1.7e-02, 1.1e-02** |
| 128 | ~2e-07 | **3.1e-04, 4.1e-02, 9.5e-03** |
| 256 | ~2e-07 | **4.7e-03, 6.7e-03, 1.0e-02** |
| 512 | ~3e-07 | **2.0e+00, 2.8e+00, 1.8e+00** |

Eager is correct throughout. Onset is **input-dependent**: `dim=64` fails for
seeds 0 and 2 but not seed 1. `dim >= 96` failed on every seed tried, `dim=32`
on none, and the error grows with the dimension.

## Scope — only LayerNorm

Each module tested individually on MPS, eager vs compiled:

| module | max diff |
|---|---|
| `nn.Linear` | 0.0 |
| `nn.GELU` | 0.0 |
| `nn.Softmax(dim=-1)` | 0.0 |
| `nn.MultiheadAttention`, no mask | 0.0 |
| `nn.MultiheadAttention`, `key_padding_mask` | 0.0 |
| **`nn.LayerNorm`** | **0.174** |
| `nn.TransformerEncoderLayer` | 0.341 — contains LayerNorm |

Other observations:

- **fp32 and fp16 are affected equally**, so this is not a precision tradeoff and is distinct from #66707 (layer_norm needing fp32 accumulation for fp16).
- Reproduces with `elementwise_affine=True` and `False`.
- `torch._dynamo.utils.counters["graph_break"]` is empty — it compiles cleanly.
- Both outputs are on `mps:0`, so it is not a silent CPU fallback.
- Eager being correct rules out the MPS "fast math" behaviour in #84936, which would affect both paths.

## Possible mechanism

The `torch.compile` on MPS tracker (#150121) notes that **multi-stage Welford reductions are not implemented**. LayerNorm computes mean and variance by a Welford reduction over `normalized_shape`, and the failure appearing between 32 and 96 elements — and worsening with size — is consistent with a reduction that is correct while it fits one stage and wrong once it needs more. #152155 reports a related multistage-reduction failure, though that one raises a shader error rather than returning wrong values.

## Related issues

- #150121 — torch.compile on MPS progress tracker (open). This probably belongs under it.
- #143182 — same symptom class, `nn.LayerNorm` silently wrong under Inductor,  but **CPU only** and **closed**, with a much smaller error (7e-4 vs 1.8).
- #150629, #150454 — RMSNorm on MPS under torch.compile: outputs zeros, and  generates invalid shaders. Adjacent normalisation-layer failures.
- #152155 — multistage reductions on MPS generating out-of-scope variables.

## Real-world impact

Found while embedding `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (6-layer BERT, hidden size 384). The compiled encoder differed from eager by **11.1 absolute** on `last_hidden_state` values spanning [-5.2, 5.3], corrupting every embedding with nothing to indicate a problem — no warning, no error, plausible-looking output.

On that model `torch.compile` was also **~7x slower** than eager (416 vs 2,885 texts/s at batch 512, fp16), so there is no speed incentive to offset the correctness risk.

The tracker does describe MPS support as an early prototype, so a failure is not surprising. Filing because this one is *silent*: a user who benchmarks `torch.compile`, sees it is slower, and moves on is fine — but a user who sees a speedup on a different model and adopts it has no signal that the numbers are wrong.

issues.title: [vllm] [triton 3.8] `tl.load(..., padding_option="zero")` on an fp8e4nv block pointer fails to compile: cannot cast int32 to fp8e4nv
issues.author: atalman

## Summary

On the **torch 2.14 nightly / triton 3.8** channel, `tests/kernels/attention/test_minimax_m3.py::test_msa_indexer_impl_matches_triton[index_dtype1-16]` fails to compile its Triton kernel:

```
triton.compiler.errors.CompilationError: at 44:8:
    if BLOCK_SIZE_Q * pid_q >= q_len:
        return
    q_ptrs = tl.make_block_ptr(
        base=q_ptr + seq_start * stride_q_n + pid_h * stride_q_h,
        shape=(q_len, head_dim),
        strides=(stride_q_n, stride_q_d),
        offsets=(pid_q * BLOCK_SIZE_Q, 0),
        block_shape=(BLOCK_SIZE_Q, head_dim),
        order=(1, 0),
    )
    q = tl.load(q_ptrs, boundary_check=(0,), padding_option="zero")
        ^

AssertionError: cannot cast int32[constexpr[64], constexpr[128]] to <['64', '128'], fp8e4nv>
```

`tl.load` with `padding_option="zero"` on a block pointer whose element type is **fp8e4nv** appears to materialize the zero-padding constant as `int32` and then fail to cast it to the pointer's fp8 element type. issues.title: @torch.compile on a class crashes under caching_precompile=True (AttributeError on '__code__')
issues.author: cjolivier01
issues.body:
Adjacent to #190659 (staticmethod) — same shape of bug on raw classes.

`@torch.compile` on a class crashes at decoration time when `caching_precompile=True`. The `caching_precompile` block in `_TorchDynamoContext.__call__` reads `fn.__code__` on the class before reaching the existing `isclass(fn)` branch, so it fails immediately with `AttributeError`.

Real-world trigger: `flash-linear-attention` decorates a `torch.autograd.Function` subclass at import time — [`fla/ops/attn/parallel.py#L726-L727`](https://github.com/fla-org/flash-linear-attention/blob/v0.5.2/fla/ops/attn/parallel.py#L726-L727). Under `caching_precompile=True` every rank dies at model build.

### Minimal repro

```python
import torch

with torch._dynamo.config.patch(caching_precompile=True):
    @torch.compile
    class Foo:
        def __call__(self, x):
            return x.sin()
```

### Error

```
AttributeError: type object 'Foo' has no attribute '__code__'
  torch/_dynamo/package.py:1007   sha256_hash.update(str(innermost_fn_.__code__.co_firstlineno)...)
  torch/_dynamo/package.py:1251   key = CompilePackage.source_id_from_fn(fn)
  torch/_dynamo/eval_frame.py:925 result = DynamoCache.load(fn_key)
```

issues.title: [inductor] ManualOverlapScheduler custom pass UUID does not include rank, causing FxGraphCache collision
issues.author: XAheli
issues.body:
## Description

`ManualOverlapScheduler` (`torch/_inductor/fx_passes/overlap_manual_scheduling.py:232`) calls `merge_all_gather_bucket` which embeds `dist.get_rank()` as a compile-time constant in the traced graph (narrow offset into the packed all-gather buffer). However, `ManualOverlapScheduler` is invoked as a custom post-grad pass (driven by torch autoparallel), so neither `bucket_all_gathers_fx` nor `enable_overlap_scheduling` configs are set.

This means the FxGraphCache key collision fix from #188332 / #191878 does not cover this path. The custom pass is hashed via a user-supplied UUID (through `_get_custom_pass_detail`), which does not carry the rank.

## Impact

When `ManualOverlapScheduler` is used via autoparallel's custom post-grad pass registration, different ranks can produce identical FxGraphCache keys despite generating different compiled code (different narrow offsets). On warm cache, one rank loads another rank's compiled artifact → CUDA driver errors.

FWIW this bug is currently **unreachable in tree**

1. `ManualOverlapScheduler` has no production usage within pytorch/pytorch (only in tests)
2. Tests always use `force_disable_caches=True`
3. Even without that the `CacheabilityValidator` (codecache.py L1125-1130) **bypasses FX cache** when `post_grad_custom_post_pass` is a plain callable (not a `CustomGraphPass` subclass)

The bug would only fire if an out-of-tree consumer wraps `ManualOverlapScheduler` in a `CustomGraphPass` with a stable `uuid()` that doesn't include rank and enables FX caching.


## Related

- Parent issue: #188332
- Fix PR (scoped to `bucket_all_gathers_fx` and `enable_overlap_scheduling`): #191878
- Noted as out-of-scope in #191878 review by @bobrenjc93

issues.title: torch._inductor.ir.FallbackKernel.find_device does not match eager behavior
issues.author: asglover
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When torch.compile exports and packages models, it uses `torch._inductor.ir.FallbackKernel.find_device` to choose a "device" for that op. 
This device is used for many things, including for naming the AOTI c-shim (`aoti_torch_{device}_{op}`) and for choosing the appropriate DeviceGuard. 
This function is inconsistent with eager mode in one primary way and one minor way. 

The primary divergence is for ops which accept Tensor args which are expected to be on different devices: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/aa8abcb98c32ef307cba9fb67839925a73ba712b/torch/_inductor/ir.py#L9595-L9599

Consider an op whose first tensor arg is on CPU but a later arg is on CUDA. 

- Eager mode considers the keys of all tensors and dispatches to the highest priority, aka CUDA
- AOTI uses the device of the first argument 

The second minor divergence is basically just future proofing the "example output"  branch.
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/aa8abcb98c32ef307cba9fb67839925a73ba712b/torch/_inductor/ir.py#L9606-L9623
Because it uses "is_gpu" instead of the backend priority list, it is incorrect for PrivateUse1 and any out of tree backend. 
(although there are lots of other blockers for using inductor this way today) 

The proposed solution is straightforward, refactor's these two bits of code to use a shared helper which implements the eager-mode backend selection logic. 

I've attached a little clauded test which shows this behavior. Let me know if you think this is behavior worth changing. The first discrepancy, `find_device(op(cpu_tensor, cuda_tensor)) = cpu` is a real bug for me. issues.title: [RFC] Inductor / AOTI tests: decouple “correct codegen path” from tight eager-fp16 equality
issues.author: iupaikov-amd
issues.body:
## 1. Summary

- Many Inductor and AOTI tests **prove two things at once**: (a) the **compiled path** matches the scenario we care about, and (b) **eager fp16** matches **compiled fp16** to a very tight tolerance. Those goals are often unrelated.
- When eager/compiled check fails on one vendor or SKU while the logic path is fine, we get **noise in CI and review**: skips, tolerance PRs, and repeated explanation - without strengthening the signal for the original regression.
- **fp16** is usually a **red herring**: the interesting question is often **routing, grid, or reference choice**, not “bit-identical GEMM across every math backend.”
- **Dedicated suites already cover fp16 matmul accuracy** (OpInfo, matmul tests). Re-encoding the same bar in **narrow integration tests** duplicates work and **varies by architecture** (e.g. different reduction tiling across GPUs).
- **Ask:** treat this as an incremental cleanup opportunity — tests that were reasonable when written can be upgraded to match the failure mode (structure, reference dtype, or codegen hints) while staying **vendor-neutral**.

---

## 2. Example: `test_bmm_large_batch_dynamic` (AOTI BMM, large dynamic batch)

- PR [#178617](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/178617) introduced logic: **dynamic** batch BMM with **`B > 65535`** must **launch legally** and **index batches correctly** (Triton batch split across `grid_y` / `grid_z`). This logic is checked by comparing if eager vs compiled outputs are bitwise identical. While this in theory covers the regression, it also is prone to 1 ULP fp16 jitter due to reordering on different archs. 
- [#183630](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/183630) scaled inputs to reduce benign fp16 noise for CUDA, which is essentially a tolerance increase in disguise. This makes the test less flaky for **some** archs, but doesn't solve the root of the issue.
- Tight **`same()`** / eager-fp16 equality is **stricter than the bug** needs and **varies by hardware** (e.g. [#179958](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/179958), [#184531](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/184531)) — **false failures** even when the **grid fix** is sound.

---

## 3. Other examples (same pattern family)

| Link | Note |
|------|------|
| [#183630](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/183630) | `test_bmm_large_batch_dynamic` — input scaling / tolerance / CUDA follow-up |

- We would like to advocate for having some sort of test design guidelines to avoid such problems in the future and help to redesign some of the existing tests. Since this problem is universal for all vendors and multitude of archs we would like to bring this to your attention. As Inductor and hardware diversity grow, **narrowing the logic** per test is a good way to move forward.
- **Proposals (pick per test):**
  - **Match logic to risk:** grid / launch bugs → **shape, finiteness, boundary indices**, optional **codegen / log substring**; fp16 GEMM agreement → **leave to OpInfo / matmul** suites or use **FP32 reference + documented tol**.

  - **Document intent in-test** (one comment): what regression file / PR motivated the scenario—helps future edits stay aligned.
- **Proposed direction:** **FP32 matmul reference** (or similar), **boundary row checks** around **65535**, optional **Inductor log / codegen hints** for the batch reconstruction — **same regression intent**, **less coupling** to eager fp16 BLAS. I will link a draft PR to highlight what was described.

issues.title: `torch.compile` vs eager DDP divergence with ResNet50 + AdamW lr=1.0 on two-node NCCL
issues.author: whitephilomel
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I see a reproducible numerical divergence between eager DDP and `torch.compile` DDP when running the same model, optimizer, seed, synthetic input tensors, and two-node NCCL setup. Both arms complete 20 optimizer steps without NaN/Inf, but the final logits fingerprint and parameter sum differ substantially.

This is not caused by dataset ordering: the reproducer uses fixed-seed synthetic tensors. AMP is disabled, TF32 is disabled, cuDNN benchmark is disabled, deterministic mode is enabled, and `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8` is used. The config contains `"precision": "bf16"`, but effective compute is fp32 because `amp_enabled=false`.

Minimal reproducer and configuration:

https://gist.github.com/whitephilomel/13d0584f7396760793b11dbbe7491dfd

## Current behavior

With PyTorch 2.9.1+cu128, two machines, one V100 GPU per machine, `world_size=2`, backend `nccl`, model `resnet50`, optimizer `adamw`, lr `1.0`, and 20 steps:

| rank | eager loss | compile loss | loss abs diff | eager grad norm | compile grad norm | grad abs diff | divergent checks |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| rank 0 | 2.3456020355 | 3.6093058586 | 1.2637038231 | 0.8535786867 | 1.0606021881 | 0.2070235014 | logits norm, logits sum, parameter sum |
| rank 1 | 2.7591028214 | 2.5354700089 | 0.2236328125 | 0.8535786867 | 1.0606021881 | 0.2070235014 | logits norm, logits sum, parameter sum |

The largest differences are in the final logits and parameter fingerprint:

| metric | eager | compile | abs diff |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| rank0 logits norm | 17.5366973877 | 34.8463401794 | 17.3096427917 |
| rank0 logits sum | 149.2867736816 | 300.2042541504 | 150.9174804688 |
| rank0 parameter sum | 379786.78125 | -98813.453125 | 478600.234375 |
| rank1 logits norm | 17.5704326630 | 34.7212409973 | 17.1508083344 |
| rank1 logits sum | 149.4028778076 | 299.1468811035 | 149.7440032959 |
| rank1 parameter sum | 379786.78125 | -98813.453125 | 478600.234375 |

## Expected behavior

For the same DDP world size, model, optimizer, initialization seed, and deterministic synthetic inputs, eager and `torch.compile` should either produce numerically close results within a reasonable tolerance or fail consistently. A large compile-only change in final logits and parameter fingerprints after successful training steps is unexpected.

### Versions

Python: 3.11.15
CUDA reported by PyTorch: 12.8
NCCL observed in confirmed runs: 2.27.5+cuda12.9

comments.author: krastogi-in
comments.body:
I agree with @shino16 and I see all Five GitHub issues ([#187444](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/187444), [#187445](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/187445), [#187446](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/187446), [#187447](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/187447), [#187448](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/187448)) reported that ResNet models trained with torch.compile + DDP produce silently different loss, gradients, and logits compared to eager mode are similar . You can even get the any one of them without ddp and backend to be inductor.

**Reason**

Inductor decomposes native_batch_norm_backward into Triton kernels that sum thousand of float32 values in a different tree order than ATen's C++ kernel. Both are mathematically correct, but float32 addition is non-associative: (a+b)+c != a+(b+c). With multiple additions, the accumulated rounding difference is ~1e-4 per element. This compounds through 20+ BN layers per backward pass, through skip connections, and across training steps — especially with Adam.

**Fix Options**

1. Accept the divergence — this is inherent to compiling reductions into GPU kernels with different accumulation order. Eager and compiled training should reach similar final accuracy, just via different trajectories.
2. Keep native_batch_norm_backward as an extern kernel in Inductor — similar to how convolution_backward is already handled. Trades fusion opportunities for bit-exact parity.
3. Use SGD or lower Adam's learning rate to reduce amplification. (Workaround.)

I think priority of the issue can be lowered as this is expected behavior. Or go with 2nd option.

### Analysis

This is a **performance regression on AArch64 CPU** that appeared after migrating the Inductor benchmark jobs to the OSDC (ARC) arm64 runners in #187994. The comparison table shows large jumps in **Abs Execution Time** while accuracy stays `pass` and **Portable speedup stays roughly constant**, e.g.:

| Model | Abs exec time (pre → post) | Approx factor |
|---|---|---|
| `mobilenetv2_100` | 52.68ms → 158.30ms | ~3.0x |
| `deit_base_distilled_patch16_224` | 308.31ms → 514.01ms | ~1.7x |
| `mobilenetv3_large_100` | 309.20ms → 481.61ms | ~1.6x |
| `repvgg_a2` | 190.96ms → 292.04ms | ~1.5x |
| `ghostnet_100` | 138.14ms → 152.06ms | ~1.1x |

**Key signal:** the *speedup* (compiled vs. eager) is essentially unchanged, and you note eager regressed by a similar amount. That points away from a `torch.compile`/Inductor codegen regression and toward the **runner environment itself** — i.e. the new ARC arm64 hosts are measuring slower wall-clock than the previous runners. Common causes for this pattern after a runner migration:

- Different/older Neoverse core generation or lower sustained clocks (no turbo / power policy)
- Fewer vCPUs or different thread/affinity defaults (`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, core pinning, NUMA)
- Noisy-neighbor / shared-host contention or thermal throttling on the new fleet
- Different glibc / kernel / BLAS (e.g. OpenBLAS vs. Arm Compute Library) or `LD_PRELOAD` / allocator differences baked into the new image

Since absolute timings are not normalized across heterogeneous hardware, a runner migration legitimately shifts the baseline. The actionable question for whoever owns the benchmark fleet is whether the new ARC arm64 runners are spec-equivalent (CPU model, core count, threading env) to the pre-migration ones, and whether a fresh baseline needs to be captured for the dashboard.

### Suggested next diagnostics
- Compare `lscpu` / `nproc` / governor and the `OMP_NUM_THREADS` + thread-affinity settings between the old and new runner images.
- Confirm the same BLAS/ACL backend and version are present in both images.
- If the new fleet is intentionally different hardware, the benchmark dashboard baseline likely needs to be re-seeded post-migration rather than treated as a code regression.

Based on the [triage rubric](.claude/skills/triaging-issues), this is a CI-infrastructure-driven performance regression on ARM (root cause is the runner migration, not PT2 codegen), so:

- `module: arm`

comments.author: huydhn
comments.body:
Root-caused and validated. The aarch64 perf runner was not on the hardware its label implied.

## Cause

`linux.arm64.m8g.metal-24xl` maps to the OSDC runner `l-barm64g4-94-344`, which was defined on a virtualized `m8g.24xlarge` as a stand-in for the real `m8g.metal-24xl`. Worse, its fleet (`m8g-large`) lists `m8g.48xlarge` at weight 100, so Karpenter was actually provisioning a **192-core / 768 GiB** node and running the 94-core job on part of it.

Graviton4 is 96 cores per socket, so `m8g.48xlarge` is two sockets / two NUMA nodes. The 94-core cgroup straddled both and paid cross-socket memory traffic on every iteration — which is exactly the kind of thing that inflates absolute wall clock while leaving the inductor-vs-eager ratio intact.

The benchmark records themselves confirm the backing. `runners[0]` from the uploaded results:

```
nightlies on main   cpu_count=192  avail_mem_in_gb=742    <- m8g.48xlarge, dual-socket
mock run on metal   cpu_count=96   avail_mem_in_gb=376    <- m8g.metal-24xl, single socket
```

## Fix and validation

pytorch/ci-infra#969 re-points the runner to a real `m8g.metal-24xl` on a dedicated single-instance fleet, so no virtualized node can be substituted in. Validated with #191823, which routes this workflow at the staging cluster where that change is deployed.

Mock run vs the median of three `main` nightlies (`inference` / `bfloat16`, config parity verified: `repeat=30, iterations=2, batch_size=None, threads=None`):

| Metric | Median delta | Improved |
|---|---|---|
| `abs_latency` | **-49.7%** | 291 / 292 models |
| `compilation_latency` | -4.0% | 230 / 286 |
| `speedup` (relative) | -3.5% | flat |

By suite, `abs_latency`: huggingface -41.6% (n=103), torchbench -73.4% (n=189).

Examples (ms, `inductor_aot_inductor`):

```
BartForCausalLM                  497.5 -> 263.4   -47%
ElectraForCausalLM               263.3 -> 133.8   -49%
M2M100ForConditionalGeneration   710.8 -> 352.2   -50%
BertForMaskedLM                  491.5 -> 273.8   -44%
AlbertForMaskedLM               1675.8 -> 1280.4  -24%
```

This reproduces the decoupling reported here, in reverse: absolute time halves while relative speedup stays flat. It also ran on *fewer* cores (92 vs 94), so this is not "more CPU".

Data: `s3://ossci-benchmarks/v3/pytorch/pytorch/{workflow_id}/`, workflow `30680927631` (metal) vs `30738497917` / `30690425905` / `30614840265` (baseline).
